Central Nervous System
Physiology
Receptors and their properties

Sensory receptors are specialized structures at the peripheral endings of afferent neurons that convert environmental energy — mechanical, thermal, chemical, or electromagnetic — into nerve impulses so the CNS can monitor internal and external change. This lesson covers how receptors are classified by stimulus type and location, the step-by-step mechanism that generates a receptor (generator) potential, the properties that distinguish it from a true action potential, and the laws governing receptor specificity (Muller's law) and stimulus-intensity coding (Weber-Fechner law). It also covers receptor adaptation — the decline in sensation with continuous stimulation — and how the CNS ultimately decodes the type, site, and intensity of any stimulus.

Definition and Function

  • Definition: specialized structures at the peripheral terminations of afferent neurons, for receiving all types of sensations and informing the CNS about any change in the external or internal environment.
  • Function: convert various forms of energy (mechanical, thermal, electromagnetic, chemical) in the environment into action potentials in the sensory nerves.

Without receptors, the CNS is functionless — every sensation the CNS interprets begins as a receptor converting a stimulus into an electrical signal.

Classification of Receptors

According to Mode of Stimulation

Receptor typeStimulusExample
MechanoreceptorsMechanicalTouch, equilibrium, auditory, and all proprioceptors (found in muscles, ligaments, joints)
ChemoreceptorsChemicalTaste, olfactory, O2 lack, CO2 excess receptors, and osmoreceptors
ElectromagneticLightOnly in the retina
ThermoreceptorsTemperatureIn the skin and hypothalamus
NociceptorsTissue damageFree nerve endings (the receptors for pain sensation)

According to Site

Exteroceptors (on the surface of the body):

  • Cutaneous receptors: in the skin — pain, touch, temperature, and pressure.
  • Teleceptors (distant/special sense receptors): detect stimuli away from the body — olfactory, visual, and auditory receptors.

Interoceptors (found inside the body, deep from the skin):

  • Proprioceptors: in deep structures — muscle, ligaments, joints, and capsules; detect position, movement, muscle tension, and relation of body parts to each other and to space.
  • Visceroceptors: in viscera — e.g., stretch receptors in the bladder, O2 lack receptors in the carotid body, and volume/baroreceptors in the heart and vascular system.
  • Hypothalamic receptors: glucoreceptors, thermoreceptors, and osmoreceptors.

Physiological Properties of Receptors

I. Excitability & the Generator Potential

Receptors respond to a stimulus by converting it into a local receptor (generator) potential, which is then carried by the connected nerve as an action potential toward the CNS. Every sensory receptor is surrounded by non-neural cells forming a sense organ — the only exceptions are free nerve endings and the membrane-bound proteins that bind chemical transmitters and hormones. Inside the sense organ's capsule, the terminal sensory nerve loses its myelin and neurolemmal sheath and continues as the first node of Ranvier, covered only by plasma membrane.

Mechanism of the generator potential:

  1. Resting state: the receptor is polarized (about −70 mV, more negative inside than outside), due to selective membrane permeability and the Na+–K+ pump.
  2. Adequate stimulation: an increase in sodium permeability produces a local depolarization at the stimulated part — the generator potential. (In Pacinian corpuscles, pressure directly opens Na+ channels, and greater pressure opens more channels.)
  3. Reaching threshold: with continuous stimulation, the local depolarization increases in magnitude until it reaches a threshold of about 10 millivolts, which depolarizes the first node of Ranvier through local current flow.
  4. Impulse generation: once depolarization is sufficient, an action potential is transmitted along the sensory nerve; the node then repolarizes, but continued stimulation depolarizes it again, producing a train of impulses. The stronger the stimulus, the larger the generator potential and the higher the impulse frequency.

Properties of the receptor potential:

  • Local, non-propagated current flow that causes depolarization of the stimulated part.
  • Duration is longer than 5 milliseconds — longer than an action potential.
  • Has no absolute refractory period.
  • Does not obey the all-or-none law.
  • Can be summated.
  • Not affected by pressure or local anesthetics.
  • Abolished by excess K+ or a deficiency of Na+ in the surrounding medium.

II. Specificity or Modality — Muller's Law of Specific Nerve Energy

Each receptor is maximally sensitive to one specific type of stimulus — its "adequate stimulus" — the one that can excite it with the least amount of energy. The sensory nerve connected to that receptor can transmit only that one type of sensation.

Example: the optic nerve transmits only light sensation, and rods/cones can also be stimulated by an inadequate stimulus (e.g., a blow to the eye), but the optic nerve still reports light — appearing as flashes. Receptors always need far more energy to respond to an inadequate stimulus than to their adequate one.

Exception: free nerve endings do not obey Muller's law. The cornea, which contains only free nerve endings, can respond to pain, touch, and temperature.

III. Effect of Stimulus Intensity — Weber-Fechner Law

The frequency of action potentials conducted along the afferent nerve fiber is directly proportional to the logarithm of the intensity of the stimulus applied to the receptor. An increase in stimulus intensity increases the amplitude of the generator potential, which in turn increases the frequency of action potentials in the afferent fiber.

Adaptation of Receptors

Definition: the decrease in the intensity of sensation due to continuous constant stimulation.
Cause: a decline in the receptor potential, or failure to keep generating action potentials at the first node of Ranvier.

Classification by Rate of Adaptation

TypeExamplesNotes / Importance
Phasic (rate) receptorsTouch and pressure receptorsAdapt rapidly; predictive function — enables the CNS to anticipate the next proper response during rapid movement (e.g., running), and abolishes prolonged unnecessary stimulation.
Moderately adapting receptorsTemperature (20–40°C), smell, and taste receptorsNo adaptation occurs for temperature below 10°C or above 45°C.
Tonic (very slowly adapting) receptorsVision, hearing, pain receptors; baro- and chemoreceptors of the carotid sinus and aortic bodiesKeep the brain aware of body status and its relation to the surroundings.

Mechanism of Adaptation

  1. Redistribution of receptor structure (Pacinian corpuscle): a suddenly applied force causes a receptor potential at one point, but within a fraction of a second the fluid inside the corpuscle redistributes so the pressure on the central nerve core becomes equal on all sides again, and the receptor potential stops.
  2. Photoreceptors of the eye: adaptation occurs through a change in the concentration of the light-sensitive photopigments.
  3. Accommodation within the nerve fiber itself: no further action potential is transmitted, caused by inactivation of Na+ channels, an increase in intracellular Ca2+, or increased activity of the Na+–K+ pump.

Adaptation vs. fatigue: receptor adaptation is different from the fatigue that occurs in skeletal muscle after prolonged exercise. Fatigue occurs more rapidly with O2 lack and is affected by the intensity of the stimulus and previous activity — adaptation is not affected by either factor.

Sensory Coding

Definition: the ability of the CNS to determine the type, site, and intensity of a stimulus.

  • Type of stimulus: determined according to Muller's law — impulses arriving from a specific receptor type are always interpreted by the sensory cortex as that one modality (e.g., impulses from cold receptors always mean "cold").
  • Site of stimulus: every part of the body is represented at a specific point in the sensory cortex, following the dermatomal distribution, so a stimulus on the leg reaches the leg area of the cortex and so on.
  • Intensity of stimulus: determined by the Weber-Fechner law — a stronger stimulus produces a greater number of action potentials, and the sensory cortex interprets a higher number of impulses as a stronger stimulus.

Compression Function of Receptors

There is a logarithmic relationship between the intensity of the stimulus, the receptor potential, and the frequency of discharge of impulses along the afferent nerve:

  • A 100-fold increase in stimulus intensity results in only about a 2-fold increase in the amplitude of the receptor potential and in the number of action potentials.
  • A 1000-fold increase in intensity leads to only about a 3-fold increase in the amplitude of the receptor potential and impulse number.

Importance: this compression enables the CNS to detect a very wide range of stimulus intensities with only a reasonable increase in the number of action potentials, saving energy for the CNS. Any single nerve theoretically cannot conduct more than 800 impulses per second, due to the absolute refractory period.

Key Points / Quick Review

Definition & Function

  • Receptors are specialized peripheral endings of afferent neurons that convert stimulus energy into nerve impulses.
  • Without receptors, the CNS is functionless.

Classification

  • By mode of stimulation: mechano-, chemo-, electromagnetic, thermo-, and nociceptors.
  • By site: exteroceptors (cutaneous, teleceptors) vs. interoceptors (proprioceptors, visceroceptors, hypothalamic receptors).

Generator Potential

  • Local depolarization from ↑ Na+ permeability; reaches a ~10 mV threshold to trigger an action potential at the first node of Ranvier.
  • Non-propagated, no absolute refractory period, doesn't obey all-or-none law, and can be summated.

Muller's Law of Specific Nerve Energy

  • Each receptor has one adequate stimulus; its connected nerve signals only that one modality, even with inadequate stimuli.
  • Free nerve endings are the exception — they respond to pain, touch, and temperature.

Weber-Fechner Law

  • Impulse frequency is directly proportional to the logarithm of stimulus intensity.

Adaptation

  • Phasic = rapid adaptation (touch/pressure), with a predictive function.
  • Moderately adapting = temperature, smell, taste.
  • Tonic = very slow/no adaptation (vision, hearing, pain, baro-/chemoreceptors).
  • Mechanisms: structural fluid redistribution, photopigment concentration change, or nerve fiber accommodation.

Sensory Coding & Compression

  • CNS decodes stimulus type (Muller's law), site (cortical map), and intensity (Weber-Fechner law).
  • Compression: a huge range of stimulus intensity produces only a small rise in impulse frequency, saving CNS energy — max ~800 impulses/second per nerve.
